w: What's tested What PTH does to calcium and phosphate Adenoma, hyperplasia or carcinoma: which is which in the parathyroid Primary versus secondary hyperparathyroidism Low PTH (hypoparathyroidism) and ignored PTH (pseudohypoparathyroidism) Salt, sugar, sex: the zones of the adrenal cortex Cushing, Conn and Addison: read the hormone with its driver Congenital adrenal hyperplasia: 21- versus 17-hydroxylase Pheochromocytoma and neuroblastoma The one idea Every gland here works by negative feedback. So in every disease, ask two things. Is the hormone high or low? And what is the thing that drives it doing? If the gland is the problem, its driver is switched off. If something else is driving the gland, both go up together. PTH in one line PTH takes back calcium and dumps phosphate. Low calcium turns PTH on. PTH makes the kidney keep calcium, lose phosphate and make active vitamin D, and it makes bone release calcium. The active end of PTH lasts only minutes. The inactive end lasts hours. The normal parathyroid Four tiny glands behind the thyroid, not in front. Two cell types: chief cells, clear to bluish, and oxyphil cells, pink. Lots of fat. The fat goes up with age. Rule of thumb: 100 minus your age is the percent of cells. At 70, it is about 70 percent fat. A 60-year-old with 80 percent cells has too many cells, and the gland may be overactive. Too much PTH, from the gland itself This is primary hyperparathyroidism. Calcium is high, PTH is high and phosphate is low. Most patients feel fine; it shows up on routine blood work. The classic triad is "stones, bones and groans": kidney stones, weak bones (osteitis fibrosa cystica) and tired muscles. Adenoma: one gland, 80 to 90 percent of cases. Usually a lower gland. Women three times more often. Hyperplasia: all four glands, 10 to 15 percent. Carcinoma: very rare. Calcium over 13. A sticky, invasive mass with necrosis. Labs cannot tell adenoma from hyperplasia. Count the glands. One big gland means adenoma: take it out. Several means hyperplasia: take out three and a half and leave half. Finding and checking the gland A sestamibi scan finds the overactive gland before surgery. At 15 minutes everything glows. At 2 hours only the bad gland still glows. During surgery, PTH is checked again. If it falls by more than half, the bad gland is out. This works because PTH lasts only minutes. Too much PTH, driven from outside This is secondary hyperparathyroidism. Something keeps calcium low, so the glands keep working. The top cause is renal failure. Low calcium and low vitamin D are the others. All the glands grow. It is milder than primary disease. Most important: fix the cause. Too little PTH, and ignored PTH Hypoparathyroidism: low PTH, so low calcium and high phosphate. Causes: thyroid surgery, DiGeorge syndrome, autoimmune disease. Signs: tetany, cramps, tingling, convulsions, laryngospasm. Chvostek sign: tap the cheek, the face twitches. Trousseau sign: squeeze the arm with a cuff, the hand spasms. Also cataracts, patchy hair loss, fragile nails, brain calcification, and dental root hypoplasia. He said that last one is important. Pseudohypoparathyroidism: pseudo means false. Calcium is low and phosphate high, but PTH is high. The body ignores PTH. These patients are short, with short hand and foot bones. First rule out kidney failure, poor absorption and low vitamin D, which look the same on labs. The adrenal: salt, sugar, sex From the outside in: glomerulosa makes aldosterone (salt), fasciculata makes cortisol (sugar), reticularis makes androgens (sex). It gets sweeter as you go in. The middle of the gland, the medulla, makes catecholamines. (He sometimes said "cortisone"; the word is cortisol.) Cushing: too much cortisol Moon face, buffalo hump, belly fat, high sugar, high blood pressure, acne, extra hair, weak bones. Check cortisol and ACTH together. Both high: ACTH is driving it, from a pituitary tumor or a tumor elsewhere such as lung cancer. Cortisol high but ACTH low: the adrenal itself is making it. Steroid pills can cause it too. Too much aldosterone Aldosterone keeps sodium and dumps potassium. Too much means high blood pressure, high sodium, low potassium and tiredness. Conn syndrome is an adrenal adenoma: aldosterone high, renin low. Secondary is from a kidney that is not getting enough blood (heart failure, a narrowed renal artery): aldosterone high and renin high. Renin tells them apart. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia Born with it, recessive, a missing enzyme on the way to cortisol. 21-hydroxylase is the common one: the path is pushed toward androgens, so too much male hormone, and a third lose salt. 17-hydroxylase is rarer: too little sex hormone, plus salt kept and high blood pressure. Treat both with glucocorticoids, which lower ACTH by feedback. Addison: the whole cortex fails Low sodium, high potassium, low blood pressure, low sugar, tiredness, weight loss, nausea, dark skin, and high ACTH. Can't handle stress. Most cases, 60 to 70 percent, are autoimmune. Others: TB and fungus, viruses, cancer spread, amyloid or iron deposits. If the pituitary is the problem instead, ACTH is low too. Adrenal tumors Most cortical adenomas make nothing; if one makes something, it is usually aldosterone. Cortical carcinomas are big, half make hormones, and most adrenal tumors that make a patient look more male are carcinomas. Pheochromocytoma: a medulla tumor that makes catecholamines. Attacks of sweating, a pounding heart and very high blood pressure. Rule of 10s: 10 percent familial, 10 percent outside the adrenal, 10 percent both sides, 10 percent malignant (he said the numbers are old). Its cells sit in little balls: Zellballen. Neuroblastoma: a very aggressive tumor of young children, 80 percent under 5. Anywhere along the sympathetic nerves, most often the belly. Spreads to bone, liver, lung and lymph nodes. "Blast" means immature. Adults can get a form in the roof of the nose.
